body.p: Claims 1 and 3-20 were previously pending. In this response, claims 1 and 4 are
amended. Therefore, following entry of the present amendments, claims 1 and 3-20 are pending.

Applicant's representatives Fredrick Tsang (Reg. No. 68,680) and Alexandra Loumidisconducted a telephonic interview with Examiner Tu on November 15, 2024. During the interview, pending claims 1, 3-20 and the rejections to those claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103 were discussed. An agreement was reached during the interview that the claims would likely overcome the cited references of record. Examiners will conduct further searching.

Claim 1 was objected to because of informalities. The Office Action states that "the electrically conductive pathways in the top set" should read as "the top set of electrically conductive pathways." The claims have been amended to recite "the parallel electrically conductive pathways in the top set" to clarify that the pathways within the set are spaced apart from each other.
Claim 1 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. § 112(b). In regard to

claim 1, the Office Action states that it is unclear how the conductive pathways form capacitors as they are electrical wiring. At [0031], the Specification describes that the electrically conductive pathways may be injected with an electrical signal that is attenuated as it passes through the dielectric layer. Claim 1 has been amended to recite "one of the top set and the bottom set of electrically conductive pathways is configured to transmit electrical signals and
another one of the top set and the bottom set of electrically conductive pathways is configured to receive the electrical signals."

Claim 4 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b). Regarding claim 4, the Office Action states that there is insufficient antecedent basis for the limitation "at least one of the electrically conductive pathways." Claim 4 has been amended to recite "at least one electronically conductive pathway of the top and bottom sets of electrically conductive pathways."
In view of the above, these rejections should be withdrawn.
The Examiner rejected claims 1, 3, 7, and 10 as obvious over the combination of
Niederkrom et al. (US 2014/0366277), Terawaki et al. (US 2011/0308019), and Bedford (US 4,847,933).
Conventional capacitive grid sensors are not air-permeable. As described at [0075] of the Specification,
Conventionally, capacitive grid sensors are produced by bonding
conductive strips to a continuous elastomer, which serves as the physical
substrate holding the conductive strips in place. This elastomer is non- permeable by design. When this style of the grid is combined with a
dielectric material to form a capacitive pressure sensor, the impermeable
elastomer substrate is present throughout the entire sensor grip area,
rendering the sensor grid layer impermeable.

In contrast to conventional capacitive grid sensors, the capacitive sensor layer recited in the claims is air-permeable. The air-permeable capacitive sensor layer includes top and bottom air-permeable substrates that carry electrically conductive pathways. The electrically conductive pathways are spaced to form horizontal air pathways and vertical air pathways, thus rendering the sensor grid air-permeable.

The cited references Niederkrom, Terawaki, and Bedford, do not recite an air-permeable capacitive sensor layer. Niederkrom, for instance, states that their pressure sensing grid is not air-permeable. At [0031], Niederkrom states:
The material properties that result in high durability of protective outer
layer 128 (e.g., to provide protection of electrical conductors 126 and

compressible dielectric 127) can result in low moisture vapor transfer rates for pressure-sensing mat 125. Moisture vapor can therefore accumulate in the interface between the person's skin and pressure mat 125. As a result,
the use of pressure-sensing mat 125 can potentially increase the likelihood
that decubitus ulcers may form on the patient.

To remedy this issue, Niederkrom does not teach to use an air-permeable pressure sensing mat. Rather, Niederkrom teaches to provide a spacer material between the pressure sensing mat and a person and to move air through the spacer material, not through the pressure sensing mat itself. See, e.g., Niederkrom at [0032]:
It may therefore be desirable to provide higher moisture vapor transfer
rates than are provided by protective outer layer 128 of pressure-sensing
mat 125. Exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure provide a
spacer material 110 and vapor permeable material 120 between pressure sensing mat 125 and a person being supported by support mattress 160.
Air mover 140 is configured to provide air flow through spacer material
and improve moisture vapor transfer, as further explained below.
Similarly, Terawaki, while describing a sensor grid, does not teach an air-permeable sensor grid, much less the air-permeable capacitive layer of the claims.
Bedford also does not teach an air-permeable capacitive layer. Bedford teaches air

channels that are throughout different layers of a foam support pad. As Niederkrom teaches to increase airflow by moving air through the spacer material 110 with an air mover 140 (see Niederkrom at [0032]), in combination with Niederkrom, Bedford would at best teach to include air channels in Niederkrom's spacer material 110 above the pressure-sensing mat 125. The combination of Bedford and Niederkrom would not teach that air-channels be included in the

pressure-sensing mat itself. Bedford in combination with Terawaki would similarly teach to include air channels in the mattress below the pressure sensing mat (see, e.g., Terawaki at [0072], "The sensor main body 30 is disposed on an upper surface of the mattress 2"), not in the pressure sensing mat itself.
In view of the above, these rejections should be withdrawn.

Based on the foregoing, the application is in condition for allowance, and reconsideration of the application is therefore requested. If the Examiner believes that direct contact would help advance prosecution of this application, the Examiner is encouraged to contact the undersigned.
The Commissioner is authorized to charge any fees due with this response to deposit account No. 19-2555, (Order Number: 29448-46781/US).
